future: Rules can improve on main without a new app download. v1 does not scrape private data and does not claim a security certification.
notes: Copy and thresholds for the beginner checklist. Detection stays in Python. Voice: warm, clear, no shame, no scores.

checks.title: Add a first file — the repo looks empty
checks.why: GitHub has a folder for this project, but there are no files yet. One file makes it real and gives you something to open tomorrow.
checks.goodEnough: Add a README that says what you are trying to make — even three sentences is enough.
checks.skipOk: If you just created the repo and are about to add files, you can ignore this.

checks.titleMissing: Write a README that says what this is
checks.titleWeak: Tell the README what this project is
checks.whyMissing: A README (say “read me”) is the first page people see. Without it, even you will forget what this folder is for.
checks.whyWeak: There is a README, but it is still just a title. A visitor cannot tell what the project does or how to try it.
checks.goodEnough: Three to five sentences: what it is, how to run it, and what “done” looks like for week one.
checks.skipOk: Skip only if this is a throwaway folder nobody else will open.

checks.title: Add a LICENSE
checks.why: A license is a short file that says how others may use your work. With no license, people have to assume they cannot copy or learn from the files.
checks.goodEnough: Pick MIT (common and friendly) using GitHub’s “Add file” helper and the license template.
checks.skipOk: Okay if you are the only person who will ever use these files.

checks.title: Double-check a secret-looking file
checks.why: We saw a file named {names}. That name often holds passwords or API keys (secret codes that let a computer into an account). This is not a security audit — just a careful look at the filename. We did not open the file.
checks.goodEnough: If the file has real secrets, remove it from the repo and put the name in a .gitignore (a list of files Git should not save). If it is empty or a template, you can ignore this.
checks.skipOk: Skip if you already know the file is a fake example.

checks.title: Add a simple .gitignore
checks.why: A .gitignore is a list of leftover files Git should not save, like .env or __pycache__. It keeps junk — and often secrets — out of the repo.
checks.goodEnough: A short list: .env, plus one line for your language (__pycache__/ for Python, node_modules/ for JavaScript).
checks.skipOk: Okay for a repo that is only markdown or docs.

checks.title: Continuous integration can wait
checks.why: CI (continuous integration) is a robot that runs checks when you save changes. Handy later. Not required to learn.
checks.goodEnough: Skip for week one. Add it when someone else will run your project, or when you have a test you want run automatically.
checks.skipOk: Skip for week one unless you are sharing with others.

checks.titleIssues: Your issue list could use a sentence each
checks.titleContributing: A short note on how people can help
checks.whyIssues: Issues are the to-do notes attached to the repo. There are {count} open. A one-line “what done looks like” on each helps future-you.
checks.whyContributing: Other people have already copied (forked) or starred this repo. A CONTRIBUTING file is a short “here is how to help” note.
checks.goodEnoughIssues: Open the oldest issue and write what “done” means in one sentence.
checks.goodEnoughContributing: Five lines: how to open an issue, and that small fixes are welcome.
checks.skipOk: Skip if you do not want help yet, or if those issues are leftover.

checks.title: The repo has been quiet — that is okay
checks.why: The last saved change (a commit is a snapshot of your files) was {when}. Projects pause. This is not a warning.
checks.goodEnough: A one-line README update is enough if you want the date to look fresh. You do not have to.
checks.skipOk: Skip if you are done with this project, or just resting.
